yawl.e: Apparently from Low German and Middle Low German jolle, or Dutch jol, possibly ultimately from a Proto-Germanic derivative of Proto-Indo-European *h₂ewlos (“tube”), see also Lithuanian aulas, Norwegian aul, Hittite [script needed] (auli-, “tube-shaped organ in the neck”), Albanian hollë, Latin alvus.

x: The “Nellie,” a cruising yawl, swung to her anchor without a flutter of the sails, and was at rest.

yawn.e:
Partly from Middle English yanen, yonen, yenen (“to yawn”), from Old English ġeonian, ġinian (“to yawn, gape”), from Proto-West Germanic *ginōn, from Proto-Germanic *ginōną (“to yawn”); and partly from Middle English gonen (“to gape, yawn”), from Old English gānian (“to yawn, gape”), from Proto-West Germanic *gainōn, from Proto-Germanic *gainōną (“to yawn, gape”); both from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰi-, *ǵʰeyh₁- (“to yawn, gape”).
Cognate with North Frisian jåne (“to yawn”), Saterland Frisian jaanj

s.d: an involuntary intake of breath through a wide open mouth; usually triggered by fatigue or boredom

s.d: The action of yawning; opening the mouth widely and taking a long, rather deep breath, often because one is tired or bored.
x: But Mrs. MacWhirr, in the drawing-room […], stifled a yawn—perhaps out of self-respect—for she was alone.

s.d: (colloquial) A particularly boring event.
x: The slideshow we sat through was such a yawn. I was glad when it finished.

s.d: utter a yawn, as from lack of oxygen or when one is tired

s.d: To open the mouth widely and take a long, rather deep breath, often because one is tired or bored, and sometimes accompanied by pandiculation.
x: I could see my students yawning, so I knew the lesson was boring them.
[…] I found my self towards Evening, first empty and sickish at my Stomach, and nearer Night mightily enclin’d to yawning and sleepy […]

s.d: To say while yawning.
x: “I haven’t the least idea what I want to do,” he yawned.
“Oh,” Sutherland yawned, “I’m too old for this.”

s.d: To present a wide opening; gape.
x: The canyon yawns as it has done for millions of years, and we stand looking, dumbstruck.
Death yawned before us, and I hit the brakes.

s.d: (obsolete) To open the mouth, or to gape, through surprise or bewilderment.
x:
[…] O heavy hour!
Methinks it should be now a huge eclipse
Of sun and moon, and that the affrighted globe
Should yawn at alteration.

[…] Hell being vnder euerie one of their Stages, the Players (if they had owed him a spight) might with a false Trappe doore haue slipt him downe, and there kept him, as a laughing stocke to al their yawning Spectators.

s.d: (obsolete) To be eager; to desire to swallow anything; to express desire by yawning.
x: to yawn for fat livings

Fly not, as thou wert wont, to his embrace,

yaws.e: Uncertain. Attested since the 1670s, perhaps from an English creole (or other language) of the Caribbean.

s.d: an infectious tropical disease resembling syphilis in its early stages; marked by red skin eruptions and ulcerating lesions

x: Other threats came from organisms co-evolving with humans, including tapeworms and such spirochaetes as Treponema, the agent of syphilis, and the similar skin infection, yaws.
